Trail: fix(login): don't close the TTY a killed Bubble Tea reader still holds
  Number:  1057
  ID:      01a001ce-4a84-7462-badc-05482f41c9fd
  Branch:  soph/fix-login-tty-race
  Base:    main
  Status:  merged
  Author:  Soph
  URL:     https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1057
  Assignees: Soph
  Type:      task
  Reviewers: paxos (approved)
  Created: 2026-08-14T19:44:51Z
  Updated: 2026-08-14T20:07:12Z

Description:
Problem:
The login prompt uses Bubble Tea for terminal input. When the CLI is cancelled via context cancellation, Bubble Tea's emergency shutdown skips waiting for its input reader goroutine to finish. This reader (on Linux, cancelreader's epoll loop) can still be reading from the TTY file descriptor after Run() returns. If the function closes the descriptor while the reader holds it, a data race occurs, and the freed file descriptor number can be reused by other code while the reader still references the closed file.
Solution:
Make TTY closing conditional. Normally the function owns and closes the descriptor. When context cancellation occurs, skip the close and leave the descriptor for process exit to reclaim. The descriptor leak is bounded—entire login is short-lived and cancels at most once per sign-in. A test verifies the descriptor stays valid after cancellation by confirming tty.Fd() returns a valid number.

content.text:
No — 1057 fixed the production bug but shipped a test that reintroduces the same race in its own teardown. It's the identical race, at the identical line.

## The two are different code paths

1057's description says it exactly: *"When context cancellation occurs, skip the close and leave the descriptor for process exit to reclaim... A test verifies the descriptor stays valid after cancellation."*

That production change is correct and holds. But the test it added to verify it does this:

```go
202: func TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen(t *testing.T) {
205: 	ptmx, tty, observer, _ := openLoginPromptPTY(t)
206: 	defer ptmx.Close()
207: 	defer observer.Close()
208: 	// Ownership stays with us on this path, so this close is the real one.
209: 	defer tty.Close()          // ← deferwrap3
```

`deferwrap3` in the race stack is that third defer — `tty.Close()`. So the test asserts the descriptor is still open, then closes it itself on the way out, while the abandoned `cancelreader` epoll goroutine is still reading `tty.Fd()`. Production stopped closing it; the test picked the close up.

That comment on line 208 is the bug in one line. Ownership *doesn't* stay with the test — the whole reason production leaks the fd is that nobody can safely own it while an unjoinable reader holds it. The test inherits that constraint and doesn't honour it.

## It failed on its own merge, the same way

1057's merge run (`31836107297`, Aug 14) failed `test-core` with the same race — same read side (`cancelreader.(*epollCancelReader).wait` → `os.(*File).Fd`), same write side:

```
Previous write at 0x00c0029c3870 by goroutine 4282:
  cli.TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen.deferwrap3()
      cmd/entire/cli/login_tty_test.go:209
```

Byte-identical to what my run hit three days later. So it landed already-flaky, and the green main runs since are just the coin coming up heads.

## Fix

Drop line 209 and correct the comment — the fd has to leak for the same reason production leaks it, and the `go test` process exit reclaims it. Lines 206–207 stay: `ptmx` is the master side and `observer` is a `dup`, so neither races the slave-side reader.

The assertion still works. `term.GetState(int(tty.Fd()))` is what proves production didn't close it, and that runs before any teardown.

That makes it a two-line change to `login_tty_test.go`. Want it as its own PR, or folded into #1981 since #1981 is already sitting in review and touching `login.go`? I'd still lean separate — it's an unrelated fix and easier to justify to a reviewer on its own.

## The flake

`test-core` fails intermittently with a data race, and because the race detector fails the whole package, one landing takes ~20 unrelated parallel tests down with it — every one reporting only `race detected during execution of test`, which hides the single real cause:

```

      cmd/entire/cli/login_tty_test.go:209
```

## Why it happens

This is the same race #2006 / trail 1057 fixed — moved from the production function into the regression test that shipped with it.

That commit (`f40fd7340`) made `readLoginURLActionFromTTY` *skip* closing the tty on the cancelled path, because Bubble Tea's `shutdown(kill=true)` skips `waitForReadLoop()`, so its `cancelreader` goroutine can outlive `Run` and keep reading `tty.Fd()` from an epoll wait loop that Bubble Tea exposes no way to join.

Its test then took the close back:

```go
// Ownership stays with us on this path, so this close is the real one.
defer tty.Close()
```

Ownership doesn't come back. The reason production leaks the descriptor is that nobody can safely own one a live unjoinable reader holds — and that is just as true in a test. So the deferred close races the reader, and whether it lands while the reader is still in its epoll wait is pure timing.

`deferwrap3` in the trace is that third defer.

- Failed on its own merge run into main: [`31836107297`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/actions/runs/31836107297) (Aug 14), same read side, same write side, same `login_tty_test.go:209`.
- Failed again three days later on an unrelated PR (#1981), byte-identical trace.
- Green main runs in between, and a rerun of #1981's failed jobs passed with zero code changes.

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

<result>## Verdict

The change is correct and the comment is well-written, but it sits one level below where the invariant belongs. The invariant is a **production** contract ("a descriptor handed to a Bubble Tea program that may be killed must never be closed"), and right now it is stated twice in prose — once in `login.go`, once in the test — and enforced nowhere. Worse, **production itself violates it on one branch**, keyed off the wrong predicate. That's the highest-value finding below.

## 1. Other sites with this hazard (the priority question)

I inventoried every Bubble Tea program and every `/dev/tty`/pty open in the repo. **No other test or production site hands a caller-closable descriptor to Bubble Tea** — but there is one production branch with the same hazard, and the "Linux-only" framing is wrong.

**A. Production, same hazard, wrong predicate — `cmd/entire/cli/login.go:763`**

`readLoginURLActionFromTTY` skips the close only when `ctx.Err() != nil` (line 746). But in bubbletea v2.0.8, `tea.go:1152`:

```go
killed := p.externalCtx.Err() != nil || p.ctx.Err() != nil || err != nil
...
p.shutdown(killed)
```

Every one of those three branches then sets `err` non-nil wrapping `ErrProgramKilled`, and the `!killed` branch leaves `err == nil`. So **`shutdown(kill=true)` ⟺ `Run()` returned a non-nil error** — a strictly wider condition than `ctx.Err() != nil`. The `err != nil` path at `login.go:763` falls through to `closeTTY == true` and closes the descriptor after a kill that abandoned the reader. Reachable sources of a non-cancel error with a live reader: `ErrProgramPanic` fed to `p.errs` from a command/renderer goroutine (`tea.go:1271`, `tea.go:1296`) and `ErrInterrupted`. With today's model (`Init` returns nil, `Update` only ever returns `tea.Quit`) this is close to unreachable, so I am **not** reporting it as a bug — I am reporting it as the altitude defect: the code expresses a proxy (`ctx.Err()`) for the real condition (`Run` returned an error / `errors.Is(err, tea.ErrProgramKilled)`), so the rule silently becomes wrong the moment the model grows a `Cmd`. Keying on `err == nil` is both simpler and exactly correct, and it makes the safe cases explicit: `initTerminal`/`initInputReader` failures return non-nil errors *before* any reader goroutine exists, so "close only when `err == nil`" is conservative, never leaky-by-mistake.

**B. The hazard is not Linux-only.** `login.go:751` and the new test comment both attribute it to "cancelreader's epoll implementation". The kqueue path is identical: `muesli/cancelreader@v0.2.2/cancelreader_bsd.go:139` does `case uint64(r.file.Fd()):` after `Kevent` returns, exactly as `cancelreader_linux.go` does after `EpollWait`. The Linux-only observation is a timing artifact, not a structural property — and the test file is `//go:build darwin || linux`, so it runs against the racy darwin reader too. The comment should say "on Linux and darwin" or drop the platform claim.

**C. Everywhere else is safe, but two of them only incidentally:**

| Site | Input | Why safe |
|---|---|---|
| `cmd/entire/cli/review/tui_sink.go:93-98` | `os.Stdin` (`review/cmd.go:1423`, `:1693`) | Calls `program.Kill()` on the escalation paths (`tui_sink.go:193`, `:310`, `:316`) — a real `shutdown(kill=true)`. Safe **only** because `os.Stdin` is never closed. Tests pass `bytes.NewReader(nil)` → `fallbackCancelReader`, which has no `Fd()` at all. |
| `investigate/tui_sink.go:32`, `activity_tui.go:74`, `search_cmd.go:245`/`:308`, `recap_tui.go:64`, `experts_tui.go:85`, `dispatch_tui.go:59` | default (`os.Stdin`, or bubbletea's own `OpenTTY()` when stdin isn't a terminal, `tea.go:1015`) | No `WithInput` of a caller-owned file; nobody closes stdin. The `OpenTTY()` descriptor is bubbletea's, and it never closes it either. |
| `strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:75-79` (`askConfirmTTY`) | `/dev/tty`, `defer tty.Close()` | Synchronous `bufio.Reader` in the calling goroutine — no background reader, so the close is unconditionally safe. |
| `login.go:97-101` (`loginURLKeysAvailable`) | `/dev/tty`, `defer tty.Close()` | Probe only (`IsTerminalReader`); no program, nothing else holds the fd. |
| `interactive/interactive.go:55-59`, `interactive/rawmode_pty_test.go` | `/dev/tty` / pty + `term.MakeRaw`/`Restore` | No Bubble Tea program; the pty test's `defer tty.Close()` races nothing. |
| All ~20 `NewAccessibleForm`/`huh` sites | default stdin, `.WithOutput(w)` only | No form is given a caller-owned tty. |

So: the answer to "is this one test the only place?" is **yes for tests, no for production** — and the review sink's safety is a coincidence of its input rather than an applied rule, which is precisely the argument for writing the rule down once.

## 2. Is a comment the right enforcement mechanism?

Not quite the ceiling, but close — the gap is small and cheap to close. What I'd do, in order of value per line:

1. **State the invariant once, at its source, in a machine-checkable form.** Change `login.go`'s `closeTTY` decision to key on `err == nil` (equivalently `!errors.Is(err, tea.ErrProgramKilled)`), which is the exact upstream signal and fixes finding 1A at the same time. Then the test comment shrinks to "production owns this descriptor and deliberately leaks it on the killed path — see `readLoginURLActionFromTTY`", instead of restating the whole rationale. One rule, one place, and the test stops being the second copy that can drift.

2. **Make the descriptor un-nameable in the test.** `openLoginPromptPTY` (`login_tty_test.go:238`) returns a bare `*os.File` named `tty` to four call sites, three of which must never close it. Return a small struct with the file unexported plus `input()` and `fd()` accessors. `defer tty.Close()` then cannot be typed by reflex — a future editor would have to write `p.input().Close()`, which reads as obviously wrong. ~15 test-only lines, no production change. Note the contract is already uniform: **all three pty tests leave the descriptor to production**, including `TestWaitForLoginURLResult_AuthCompletionCancelsTTYAndRestoresTerminal`, which also goes through the ctx-cancel/kill path. So the helper can enforce "never closable by the caller" with zero exceptions.

3. **Skip these two:** a `forbidigo` rule (the repo's precedent at `.golangci.yaml:104-121` is for package-level API bans like `Worktree.Status`; banning `^tty\.Close$` is text-matching a local variable name — brittle and it would not have caught this written as `p.input().Close()`), and widening the production parameter to an interface so tests can inject a Close-counting wrapper (changes production shape purely for test benefit; the assertion it buys is worth less than the accessor in option 2).

A `t.Cleanup` that "closes only on the paths where production closes" is not implementable: the helper cannot know which path the test will take, and on the graceful path production already closed it, so the cleanup would be a no-op double-close with no value.

## 3. Is the real problem upstream? (yes, and one claim in the comment is wrong)

test(login): stop the cancelled-TTY test closing the fd it asserts is open

TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen closed the
descriptor in teardown, which is the same data race the production fix in
f40fd7340 exists to avoid — just moved from the function into its own
regression test.

That commit made readLoginURLActionFromTTY skip the close on the cancelled
path, because Bubble Tea's shutdown(kill=true) skips waitForReadLoop() and
its cancelreader goroutine can outlive Run, reading tty.Fd() from a wait
loop that cannot be joined. The test then took the close back:

	// Ownership stays with us on this path, so this close is the real one.
	defer tty.Close()

Ownership does not come back — nobody can safely own a descriptor a live
unjoinable reader holds, in a test no less than in production. So the
deferred close raced the reader, and because the race detector fails the
whole package, one landing took ~20 unrelated parallel tests down with it:

	Read at 0x00c00088a730 by goroutine 11009:
	  os.(*File).Fd()
	  cancelreader.(*epollCancelReader).wait()  cancelreader_linux.go:147
	Previous write at 0x00c00088a730 by goroutine 4290:
	  internal/poll.(*FD).destroy()
	  os.(*File).Close()
	  ...CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen.deferwrap3()  login_tty_test.go:209

Timing-dependent, so it landed already-flaky: it failed on its own merge run
(31836107297) and again three days later on an unrelated PR, with green main
runs in between.

Only observed on Linux, but the hazard is not Linux-specific and the doc
comment no longer claims it is: cancelreader reads file.Fd() after each wake
on both backends — cancelreader_linux.go:147 after EpollWait, and
cancelreader_bsd.go:139 after Kevent — and this file builds on darwin too.
Which platform trips the detector is luck, not structure.

Drop the close. Rather than only describing the rule, enforce it: t.Cleanup
runs after the test body's deferred closes, so asserting the descriptor is
still open from there fails deterministically, on every platform, if anyone
re-adds a close — instead of waiting for the detector to catch it on a

Only ever *observed* on Linux, but the hazard is not Linux-specific, and the doc comment no longer claims it is. `cancelreader` reads `file.Fd()` after each wake on both backends — `cancelreader_linux.go:147` after `EpollWait`, `cancelreader_bsd.go:139` after `Kevent` — and this file builds on darwin too (`//go:build darwin || linux`). Which platform trips the detector is luck, not structure.

## The fix

Drop the close. Rather than only *describing* the rule, enforce it.

`t.Cleanup` runs after the test body's deferred closes, so asserting from there that the descriptor is still open fails **deterministically, on every platform**, the moment anyone re-adds a close — instead of waiting for the race detector to catch it on some future Linux CI run and get blamed on an unrelated PR, which is exactly what happened twice already.

Verified in both directions before committing: the assertion passes as written, and fails with `bad file descriptor` once a `defer tty.Close()` is restored. The same closure serves the original in-body assertion, so the two checks now name which moment closed it.

Three things worth noting:

- **The original assertion still runs where it did.** `term.GetState(int(tty.Fd()))` after the call is what proves production didn't close the descriptor; the cleanup adds the teardown half.
- **The sibling tests already omit this close**, because production *does* close the tty on their (non-cancelled) path. This makes the cancelled test consistent with them.
- **`ptmx` and `observer` stay closed** — different descriptors, so neither touches the `*os.File` the reader still holds. (`observer` is a `unix.Dup`, so a distinct fd number over the same open file description; distinct enough that closing it doesn't disturb the reader.)

The fd leaks for the test binary's lifetime, the same bounded trade production already makes.

## Verification

`mise run lint` clean and `go test -race ./cmd/entire/cli/` green, plus the TTY tests at `-count=3`. Note what local runs can and can't show: they confirm nothing broke and that the tripwire fires, but they cannot prove the race is gone, because whether it reproduces is timing-dependent on either platform. The structural argument is that the only close of that descriptor is gone, and the race trace had no other write site.

## The flake

`test-core` fails intermittently with a data race, and because the race detector fails the whole package, one landing takes ~20 unrelated parallel tests down with it — every one reporting only `race detected during execution of test`, which hides the single real cause:

```
Read at 0x00c00088a730 by goroutine 11009:
  os.(*File).Fd()
  cancelreader.(*epollCancelReader).wait()      cancelreader_linux.go:147
  bubbletea/v2.(*Program).readLoop()

Previous write at 0x00c00088a730 by goroutine 4290:
  internal/poll.(*FD).destroy()
  os.(*File).Close()
  cli.TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen.deferwrap3()
      cmd/entire/cli/login_tty_test.go:209
```

## Why it happens

This is the same race #2006 / trail 1057 fixed — moved from the production function into the regression test that shipped with it.

That commit (`f40fd7340`) made `readLoginURLActionFromTTY` *skip* closing the tty on the cancelled path, because Bubble Tea's `shutdown(kill=true)` skips `waitForReadLoop()`, so its `cancelreader` goroutine can outlive `Run` and keep reading `tty.Fd()` from an epoll wait loop that Bubble Tea exposes no way to join.

Its test then took the close back:

```go
// Ownership stays with us on this path, so this close is the real one.
defer tty.Close()
```

Ownership doesn't come back. The reason production leaks the descriptor is that nobody can safely own one a live unjoinable reader holds — and that is just as true in a test. So the deferred close races the reader, and whether it lands while the reader is still in its epoll wait is pure timing.

`deferwrap3` in the trace is that third defer.

## Evidence it landed already-flaky

- Failed on its own merge run into main: [`31836107297`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/actions/runs/31836107297) (Aug 14), same read side, same write side, same `login_tty_test.go:209`.

Drop the close, and explain why so it doesn't get added back. The fd leaks for the test binary's lifetime — the same bounded trade production already makes — and process exit reclaims it.

- **The assertion is unaffected.** `term.GetState(int(tty.Fd()))` is what proves production didn't close the descriptor, and it runs before any teardown.
- **The sibling tests already omit this close**, because production *does* close the tty on their (non-cancelled) path. This makes the cancelled test consistent with them.
- **`ptmx` and `observer` stay closed.** `ptmx` is the master side and `observer` is a `unix.Dup`, so both are separate descriptors and neither touches the `*os.File` the reader still holds.

content.text:
Four reviews done, findings applied to PR #2009 (`13de017d9`, force-pushed — my branch, one commit, no reviewers yet). CI is running on the amended commit.

## A correction first

I told you twice that this race was **Linux-only** because "darwin's cancelreader uses a different implementation." The altitude review challenged it and was right — I checked:

```
cancelreader_linux.go:147   case int32(r.file.Fd()):     // after EpollWait
cancelreader_bsd.go:139     case uint64(r.file.Fd()):    // after Kevent
```

Both read `file.Fd()` after waking; `cancelreader_bsd.go` builds on darwin, and the test file is `//go:build darwin || linux`. Different *implementation*, identical *hazard*. Which platform trips the detector is luck. That claim was in the commit message and PR body, so both are corrected.

## Fixed

**Comment volume** (converged: reuse + simplification). My 11-line comment restated what the doc comment 7 lines above and `login.go` already said — three copies of one mechanism, one commit apart. Trimmed to the single non-obvious fact: *teardown is not late enough*.

**Dropped the ptmx/observer paragraph.** It defended lines nobody questioned, and was loose: `observer` is a `unix.Dup`, so a distinct fd *number* over the *same* open file description — not a "separate descriptor" as I wrote. Kept the accurate version as a parenthetical in the PR body only.

**Replaced prose with a tripwire** (the altitude finding — "is a comment the right enforcement mechanism?"). `t.Cleanup` runs after the body's deferred closes, so asserting there that the fd is still open fails **deterministically on every platform** if anyone re-adds the close, rather than waiting for the detector to catch it on Linux CI and get misattributed — which happened twice. I verified both directions before committing: passes as written, fails with `bad file descriptor` once a `defer tty.Close()` is restored. One closure now serves both assertions, so each names which moment closed it.

**Platform claim in the doc comment** — now "epoll on Linux, kqueue on darwin."

## Skipped, and worth your attention

The altitude review surfaced two things in **production** that are real but outside a test-flake fix. I did not touch them:

1. **`closeTTY` keys on the wrong predicate.** `login.go:746` skips the close when `ctx.Err() != nil`, but bubbletea's kill condition is `externalCtx.Err() != nil || ctx.Err() != nil || err != nil` — strictly wider. The `err != nil` branch closes after a kill that abandoned the reader. Near-unreachable today (the model only ever returns `tea.Quit`), but it becomes wrong the moment that model grows a `Cmd`. Keying on `err == nil` is both simpler and exactly right.
2. **`login.go:756` is inaccurate**: "Bubble Tea exposes nothing to join that goroutine." `ReleaseTerminal()` → `releaseTerminal(false)` does call `Cancel()` then `waitForReadLoop()`. The conclusion survives (it returns no result, so you get no proof it joined), but the stated reason is wrong.

Also skipped: the `openLoginPromptPTY` cleanup-ownership refactor and the accessor-struct variant (both expand a targeted fix across four call sites), and a CLAUDE.md entry — which I'd hold until #1 lands, since documenting a rule the code implements with the wrong predicate would enshrine something half-true.

One more finding I'd flag as the more interesting one: the "one exception" framing in both comments undersells reality. Auth completion calls `cancelAction()`, which drives the *cancelled* path — so **every successful login where the user doesn't press a key leaks a descriptor**. Bounded to one per sign-in, but it's the normal path, not an edge case.

Those are all one small production PR together. Want it?

## The flake

`test-core` fails intermittently with a data race, and because the race detector fails the whole package, one landing takes ~20 unrelated parallel tests down with it — every one reporting only `race detected during execution of test`, which hides the single real cause:

```
Read at 0x00c00088a730 by goroutine 11009:
  os.(*File).Fd()
  cancelreader.(*epollCancelReader).wait()      cancelreader_linux.go:147
  bubbletea/v2.(*Program).readLoop()

Previous write at 0x00c00088a730 by goroutine 4290:
  internal/poll.(*FD).destroy()
  os.(*File).Close()
  cli.TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen.deferwrap3()
      cmd/entire/cli/login_tty_test.go:209
```

## Why it happens

This is the same race #2006 / trail 1057 fixed — moved from the production function into the regression test that shipped with it.

That commit (`f40fd7340`) made `readLoginURLActionFromTTY` *skip* closing the tty on the cancelled path, because Bubble Tea's `shutdown(kill=true)` skips `waitForReadLoop()`, so its `cancelreader` goroutine can outlive `Run` and keep reading `tty.Fd()` from an epoll wait loop that Bubble Tea exposes no way to join.

Its test then took the close back:

```go
// Ownership stays with us on this path, so this close is the real one.
defer tty.Close()
```

Ownership doesn't come back. The reason production leaks the descriptor is that nobody can safely own one a live unjoinable reader holds — and that is just as true in a test. So the deferred close races the reader, and whether it lands while the reader is still in its epoll wait is pure timing.

`deferwrap3` in the trace is that third defer.

## Evidence it landed already-flaky

- Failed on its own merge run into main: [`31836107297`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/actions/runs/31836107297) (Aug 14), same read side, same write side, same `login_tty_test.go:209`.
- Failed again three days later on an unrelated PR (#1981), byte-identical trace.
- Green main runs in between, and a rerun of #1981's failed jobs passed with zero code changes.

Only ever *observed* on Linux, but the hazard is not Linux-specific, and the doc comment no longer claims it is. `cancelreader` reads `file.Fd()` after each wake on both backends — `cancelreader_linux.go:147` after `EpollWait`, `cancelreader_bsd.go:139` after `Kevent` — and this file builds on darwin too (`//go:build darwin || linux`). Which platform trips the detector is luck, not structure.

## The fix

Drop the close. Rather than only *describing* the rule, enforce it.

`t.Cleanup` runs after the test body's deferred closes, so asserting from there that the descriptor is still open fails **deterministically, on every platform**, the moment anyone re-adds a close — instead of waiting for the race detector to catch it on some future Linux CI run and get blamed on an unrelated PR, which is exactly what happened twice already.

Verified in both directions before committing: the assertion passes as written, and fails with `bad file descriptor` once a `defer tty.Close()` is restored. The same closure serves the original in-body assertion, so the two checks now name which moment closed it.

Three things worth noting:

- **The original assertion still runs where it did.** `term.GetState(int(tty.Fd()))` after the call is what proves production didn't close the descriptor; the cleanup adds the teardown half.
- **The sibling tests already omit this close**, because production *does* close the tty on their (non-cancelled) path. This makes the cancelled test consistent with them.
- **`ptmx` and `observer` stay closed** — different descriptors, so neither touches the `*os.File` the reader still holds. (`observer` is a `unix.Dup`, so a distinct fd number over the same open file description; distinct enough that closing it doesn't disturb the reader.)

The fd leaks for the test binary's lifetime, the same bounded trade production already makes.

## Verification

`mise run lint` clean and `go test -race ./cmd/entire/cli/` green, plus the TTY tests at `-count=3`. Note what local runs can and can't show: they confirm nothing broke and that the tripwire fires, but they cannot prove the race is gone, because whether it reproduces is timing-dependent on either platform. The structural argument is that the only close of that descriptor is gone, and the race trace had no other write site.

content.text:
The efficiency review came in last and was the most consequential. PR #2009 updated (`89a3d947e`).

## It found that my fix doesn't fully fix the flake

I reproduced this myself on darwin at `-count=2000` rather than take it on trust — **a second racing pair survives, entirely upstream:**

```
os.(*File).Close()
  cancelreader.(*kqueueCancelReader).Close()   cancelreader_bsd.go:109
os.(*File).Fd()
  cancelreader.(*kqueueCancelReader).wait()    cancelreader_bsd.go:141
```

`cancelreader`'s `Close()` closes its own cancel-signal pipe while a still-blocked `wait()` reads that pipe's `Fd()`. Same shape as the bug I fixed, different descriptor, and **no frame from this repo** — it's present on both backends (`bsd:109/141`, `linux:118/150`).

So the honest claim is narrower than "fixes the flake": this removes *our* contribution to it. `test-core` can still flake, more rarely. I put a triage rule in the PR and commit message — if a future trace names `login_tty_test.go` it's a regression of this PR; if it names only `cancelreader`, it's upstream and wants a patch to `muesli/cancelreader` (cache both fds at construction) or to bubbletea (join the read loop on the kill path).

That also means the reproduction was **on darwin**, independently confirming the correction I made earlier — this was never Linux-only.

## Also corrected

I wrote that the fd "leaks for the test binary's lifetime." Measurably wrong: `os.newFile` registers a finalizer (`os/file_unix.go:225`), and the abandoned `*os.File` becomes unreachable once the reader exits, so the GC reclaims it. The leak is smaller than I claimed.

## Non-findings worth keeping

The review measured the things I'd have hand-waved: the abandoned goroutine **blocks** (all three backends wait with no timeout, `EINTR` is the only `continue`) and drains in ~40µs, max 2 extra goroutines — so no CPU tax on later tests. `ptmx.Close()` is a backstop, not the mechanism; `Cancel()`'s pipe write is what ends the reader. And fd exhaustion is impossible — Go raises `RLIMIT_NOFILE` to the hard limit at startup, so shell `ulimit -n` is irrelevant. It also confirmed `Program.Wait()` genuinely can't help: `p.finished` is closed by a `defer` inside `Run`.

Full `/simplify` outcome across the four angles: comment volume trimmed (3 copies → 1), the imprecise ptmx/observer paragraph dropped, prose replaced with a verified tripwire, platform claim fixed, leak cost corrected, residual race disclosed. Skipped and flagged for a separate production PR: the `closeTTY` predicate keying on `ctx.Err()` instead of `err == nil`, the inaccurate `ReleaseTerminal` comment, the "one exception" framing (auth completion makes the leak the *normal* path), and a CLAUDE.md entry.

CI is running on the amended commit.

content.text:
CI caught a bug I introduced. Fixed and pushed as `14afae09d`.

## What broke

The tripwire I added during `/simplify` failed on Linux:

```
--- FAIL: TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen
    login_tty_test.go:214: tty was closed during teardown: input/output error
```

`input/output error` — **EIO, not EBADF**. Nothing closed the tty. My cleanup used `term.GetState` (tcgetattr) on the slave, and by the time it ran, the deferred `ptmx.Close()` had revoked the pty master. On Linux that makes tcgetattr on the slave return EIO even though the descriptor is perfectly open. A false positive.

My local probe passed because darwin's tcgetattr still succeeds after the master closes. I verified the tripwire in both directions — but only on one platform, on the exact axis where this whole bug has been platform-sensitive. That's the same mistake in miniature as the "Linux-only" claim earlier.

## The fix

Check the descriptor **number** instead of the terminal state:

```go
t.Cleanup(func() {
	if int(tty.Fd()) < 0 {
		t.Error("tty was closed during teardown")
	}
})
```

`Close` sets `fd.Sysfd = -1` in `internal/poll.(*FD).destroy` — shared, non-platform-specific code — so this is platform-independent by construction rather than by observation. The pty master's state is irrelevant to it. Verified again both ways on darwin: passes as written, fails with `tty was closed during teardown` when a `defer tty.Close()` is restored.

The original in-body `term.GetState` assertion is back exactly as it was upstream — it runs *before* teardown, so the revoked-master problem never applies there, and it keeps its precise message about the cancelled path.

Both the code comment and the commit message now record why the fd-number check is the right probe and how the terminal-state version failed, so nobody re-introduces it.

## Status

Three force-pushes on this branch now, all pre-review, and the commit message has accumulated real substance: the residual upstream race with its triage rule, the corrected leak cost, and now the probe rationale. CI is running on `14afae09d`; I'll report when `test-core` lands.

Two things still open from before, both yours to call: the production `closeTTY` PR (wrong predicate, inaccurate `ReleaseTerminal` comment, "one exception" framing, CLAUDE.md entry), and #1981 needing a trail approval.

CI is green on `14afae09d` — `test-core` included, which is the job the fd-number probe had to survive on Linux.

## Both PRs are now code-complete and blocked only on review

| | PR | GitHub checks | Blocker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows browser launch | [#1981](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1981) | all pass | trail 1037 — no approvals |
| TTY test flake | [#2009](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2009) | all pass | trail 1058 — no approvals |

`Entire Gates` is the only red mark on either, and on both it's the approval gate at 0s, not a test.

## Worth knowing about #2009 before you approve it

The final commit message carries three things that took real work to establish, and they matter for how you read a future failure:

- **It doesn't eliminate the flake.** A second racing pair survives in `muesli/cancelreader` — `Close()` on its cancel-signal pipe versus a blocked `wait()` reading that pipe's `Fd()`. I reproduced it on darwin at `-count=2000`. The commit carries a triage rule: a trace naming `login_tty_test.go` is a regression of this PR; a trace naming only `cancelreader` is upstream.
- **The race was never Linux-only** — both backends read `file.Fd()` after waking, and the test builds on darwin. I'd told you otherwise twice; that's corrected in the code comment, commit, and PR body.
- **The tripwire probes the fd number, not terminal state.** My first version used `tcgetattr` and failed on Linux CI with EIO because the deferred `ptmx.Close()` had revoked the pty — a false positive on a perfectly open descriptor. The reason is now in the comment so it doesn't come back.

## Still open, in the order I'd do them

1. **Production follow-up PR** — `closeTTY` keys on `ctx.Err() != nil`, but bubbletea's kill condition is wider (`err != nil`), so one branch closes after a kill that abandoned the reader. Near-unreachable today, wrong the moment the model grows a `Cmd`. Bundle with the inaccurate `ReleaseTerminal` comment, the "one exception" framing (auth completion makes the leak the normal path), and the CLAUDE.md entry.
2. **The `/dev/tty`-on-Windows probe** — still the open question behind the original bug report. Your colleague's clean VM and Ravikanth's dev box disagreed, and the leading hypothesis is a stray `C:\dev\tty` making the probe succeed by accident. One `Test-Path C:\dev\tty` from the reporter settles it; the `test-windows` job can answer the stock-runner half.

content.text: "Proper fix" could point at three different things we've uncovered, and they're in different subsystems — so let me confirm rather than guess wrong.

questions.question: Which root cause do you want fixed properly?

options.label: Windows TTY detection (Recommended)
options.description:
Replace the /dev/tty probe in interactive.CanPromptInteractively() with term.IsTerminal on the console handle (x/term already ships term_windows.go using GetConsoleMode, and the repo already calls it in IsTerminalWriter).

This is the root cause behind the original bug report: on Windows the probe resolves to C:\dev\tty, so it fails on a clean box and succeeds by accident on one that happens to have that path — which is why your colleague's VM and Ravikanth's machine disagreed. Open /dev/tty once per login in loginURLInteractor instead of once per read, and never close it — which deletes the conditional-close invariant entirely, along with the comment, the tripwire, and the fd-scaling concern (today a user mashing 'c' re-arms a fresh descriptor per keypress).

options.label: Upstream the cancelreader fix

Patch the residual race at its source, so it stops costing everyone CI flakes.

Slowest to land, and out of our control once filed.

## The flake

`test-core` fails intermittently with a data race, and because the race detector fails the whole package, one landing takes ~20 unrelated parallel tests down with it — each reporting only `race detected during execution of test`, which hides the single real cause.

It has hit main twice: on the merge run of #2006 (`31836107297`, Aug 14) and again three days later on an unrelated PR (#1981), with green main runs in between.

## One cause, two racing pairs

bubbletea's `shutdown` does this:

```go
if p.cancelReader.Cancel() {
	if !kill {
		p.waitForReadLoop()
	}
}
_ = p.cancelReader.Close()
```

On a **killed** `Run` it skips the join, so `Close` lands while the input reader may still be inside `wait()`. That reader reads two descriptors on wake:

1. **`tty.Fd()`** — ours. This is the pair #2006 designed around by leaking the descriptor, and the pair its regression test then re-created by closing that descriptor in teardown.
2. **`cancelSignalReader.Fd()`** — cancelreader's own cancel-signal pipe, which `Close()` closes (`cancelreader_bsd.go:109`, `cancelreader_linux.go:118`) while `wait()` reads it (`:141`, `:150`). Entirely upstream; nothing on our side can avoid it.

And `Run` treats a cancelled context as killed:

```go
killed := p.externalCtx.Err() != nil || p.ctx.Err() != nil || err != nil
```

So passing `ctx` to `tea.WithContext` made **every** cancellation take the racy path. That matters more than it sounds: cancellation is the *normal* path here, not an edge case — `waitForLoginURLResult` cancels the reader as soon as authentication completes, so every sign-in where the user doesn't press a key went through it.

## The fix: stop cancelling, start quitting

`Quit` delivers a `QuitMsg`, which `eventLoop` returns with a **nil** error, so `killed` stays false and `shutdown` joins the read loop before closing anything. Nothing holds either descriptor by the time they're closed — which kills **both** pairs, including the upstream one, without patching upstream.

It also means `tty` can simply be closed on the cancelled path rather than leaked, so the conditional close, the long comment, the teardown tripwire, and the leak all go away.

**Not a bare swap.** `Quit` sends on an unbuffered channel, so an event loop that never takes it would block `Quit` forever — and `finishActionRead` (`login.go:615`) joins this read once authentication completes, so a hang there would strand a *completed* sign-in. That's a worse failure than the leak being removed. bubbletea therefore keeps its own context, cancelled only if the graceful path doesn't land within `loginURLQuitGrace`, and the descriptor is left alone in exactly that case — keyed on `tea.ErrProgramKilled`, the upstream signal, rather than on a proxy for it.

## Verification

On darwin under `-race`:

| Load | Races before | Races after |
|---|---|---|
| 2000× the cancelled test | reproduced the cancelreader pair | **0** |
| 2×1500× every TTY test | — | **0** |

Plus `go test -race ./cmd/entire/cli/`, `mise run test:ci`, and `mise run lint` all green.

The before/after comparison is the load-bearing evidence here: the same 2000-iteration run that reliably surfaced the upstream pair on the previous commit is now clean, which is what distinguishes this from the partial fix.

## Test change

`TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_CancelledLeavesDescriptorOpen` becomes `_CancelledClosesDescriptor`. Its premise inverted — the cancelled path now owns the descriptor like every other path. It asserts on the descriptor *number* (`Close` sets `Sysfd` to -1 in `internal/poll.(*FD).destroy`, so it's platform-independent) rather than terminal state, which would report EIO on Linux merely because `ptmx` is still open.

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,

bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix

<result>## Verdict

The fix is correct and at the right *file*, but one level too low to be durable, and it leaves one other site with the same unfixed upstream hazard. Most importantly: an upstream fix already landed for the sibling half of this exact race, which makes the remaining half a one-line upstream change that would delete this workaround entirely.

Note first: the working tree is **not** the committed diff. `cmd/entire/cli/login.go` is dirty with an uncommitted variant marked `// EXPERIMENT: Program.Kill() instead of a killCtx` (`context.AfterFunc` + `time.AfterFunc(loginURLQuitGrace, program.Kill)`, lines 751-763). I reviewed the committed diff as instructed. Both variants land in the same place (`Kill()` *is* `shutdown(true)`; a cancelled `killCtx` makes `Run` call `shutdown(true)`), so the altitude analysis applies to either.

## 1. Other sites — full enumeration

Verified against `charm.land/bubbletea/v2@v2.0.8`. The hazard needs two things: reaching `shutdown(kill=true)` (which skips `waitForReadLoop()` at `tea.go:1250-1256` but still calls `cancelReader.Close()`), and something closable held by the reader.

| Site | cancellable ctx to tea? | Kill()? | input | closable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cmd/entire/cli/activity_tui.go:74` | no | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/recap_tui.go:64` | no | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/search_cmd.go:245` | no | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/search_cmd.go:308` | no | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/experts_tui.go:85` | no | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/dispatch_tui.go:59` | no | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/investigate/tui_sink.go:32` | no (`Quit()` on ctx, :73) | no | default | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/review/tui_sink.go:93` | no | **yes — :193, :310, :316** | `os.Stdin` (`review/cmd.go:1423,1693`) | no |
| `cmd/entire/cli/login.go:762` | yes (killCtx) | via killCtx | owned `/dev/tty` | **yes** |
| ~44 × `form.RunWithContext(ctx)` | **yes** (`huh/v2@v2.0.3 form.go:694` appends `tea.WithContext(ctx)`) | no | default | no |

**Finding 1 (highest value): `cmd/entire/cli/review/tui_sink.go:193`, `:310`, `:316` take `shutdown(kill=true)` deliberately, and the upstream cancel-pipe race applies there too.** The `tea.WithInput` descriptor is `os.Stdin`, which the process never closes, so the *application-level* fd race does not apply. But the second race the diff describes is entirely internal to cancelreader and independent of who owns the input: `Close()` closes `cancelSignalReader`/`Writer` (`cancelreader_bsd.go:105-109`, `cancelreader_linux.go`, `cancelreader_select.go`) while the still-live read loop reads `cancelSignalReader.Fd()` in `wait()` (`cancelreader_bsd.go:141`) and, on the ErrCanceled branch, `Read`s it. Any `File` input takes a real (kqueue/epoll/select) reader with that pipe; only a non-`File` input gets the no-op `fallbackCancelReader`. So `entire review` on a real terminal hits it whenever a wedged loop escalates to `Kill()` — the very scenario `tuiSinkQueueCap`'s comment documents as observed live. Blast radius is small (it happens immediately before process exit), but it is the same hazard, unfixed, and undocumented at that site. It is also **untestable as currently written**: `review/tui_sink_test.go` passes `bytes.NewReader(nil)`, which routes to the fallback reader whose `Close()` is a no-op, so `-race` will never catch it there.

**Finding 2: the other sites' safety is incidental, not by rule.** Nobody else passes `tea.WithInput` with an owned descriptor (`login.go:765` is the only such call in the repo), and bubbletea never closes its own input — it takes `os.Stdin` or opens a TTY itself at `tea.go:1010-1018` and only *restores* state at `tty.go:39-52`, never closes. So the fd can't be freed under a reader anywhere else. Nothing enforces or records that; the next author who writes `tea.WithInput(myTTY)` reproduces the bug.

**Finding 3: the invariant cannot be stated as "never hand bubbletea a cancellable context."** 44 `form.RunWithContext(ctx)` sites already do exactly that, unavoidably — huh offers no other API. The real invariant is narrower: *never let a bubbletea program take the kill path while you own a descriptor it is reading.* If the rule is written down, it has to be written that way or it will read as already-violated-in-44-places and be ignored.

**Finding 4 (altitude, not a bug): five different cancellation designs across nine programs.** `investigate` watches ctx → `Quit()` with no escalation (a wedged loop hangs `Wait()` forever, `tui_sink.go:82-90`). `review` enqueues a quit msg → 2s → `Kill` → 2s → abandon. `login` (new) → `Quit` → 2s → kill ctx. `activity`/`recap`/`search`/`experts` accept a `ctx` and never wire it to the program at all — they survive SIGINT only because they leave bubbletea's signal handler enabled (unlike the three that pass `WithoutSignalHandler`), so cobra-ctx cancellation leaves their TUI up. This branch adds the fifth variant.

## 2. Right layer? A shared wrapper is the better altitude

Yes — a wrapper is justified, but on the strength of Finding 4, not Finding 1. The fd concern alone is a one-site problem and doesn't pay for an abstraction. The *shape* concern does: nine programs, five hand-rolled shutdown protocols, two of which (investigate's unbounded wait, the four unwired ones) are worse than the one being fixed here.

A `uiform.RunProgram(ctx, model, opts...)` — `uiform` already exists for precisely this purpose ("Centralises the Theme()+WithAccessible() recipe so picker UI stays consistent across callers") — that does graceful-Quit-then-bounded-escalate would: make the hazard unreachable by construction, since no caller ever writes `tea.WithContext` again; collapse review's hand-rolled escalation and investigate's unbounded wait into one implementation; and wire ctx into the four programs that currently ignore it. The escalation constant then lives once instead of being independently rediscovered as `tuiPostRunCompleteGrace = 2s` (review) and `loginURLQuitGrace = 2s` (login) — note both landed on the same 2s independently, which is itself the argument.

Enforcement is cheap and has direct precedent: `.golangci.yaml:104-121` already runs `forbidigo` with `analyze-types: true` and five rules of exactly this shape (`Worktree.Status`, go-git `Reset`/`Checkout`, cobra `Print*`). A `tea.WithContext` / `(*tea.Program).Kill` rule pointing at the wrapper is a drop-in, and it is the only thing that actually stops the future author the review question anticipates.

I would not gate this fix on the wrapper. Land the fix, then extract — but extract, because the fix as written is the fifth variant of a pattern that should have one.

## 3. Upstream — this is the real fix, and it deletes the workaround

**An upstream issue exists and is closed: [charmbracelet/bubbletea#1599](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/issues/1599)**, "v2: data race between cancelreader.Close() and cancelreader.wait() during shutdown", filed 2026-02-26 by julez-dev, describing this exact race pair verbatim ("the write is `epollCancelReader.Close()` closing `cancelSignalReader` ... the read is `epollCancelReader.wait()` calling `cancelSignalReader.Fd()`").

The important part: **it was closed by fixing only half of it.** The root cause it named was `ultraviolet.TerminalReader.StreamEvents` returning on `<-ctx.Done()` without joining its inner `streamData` goroutine. That is fixed in the pinned ultraviolet — `terminal_reader.go:163-170` now does `wg.Wait()` on both exits. I confirmed the fix landed between pins: `ultraviolet@v0.0.0-20251205161215` has no `wg.Wait()`; `@20260416155717` onward (including the pinned `@20260703014108`) does.

With that fix, `shutdown(kill=false)` is now genuinely safe: `p.cancel()` → `StreamEvents` joins `streamData` (unblocked by `Cancel()`'s pipe write) → `readLoopDone` closes → `waitForReadLoop` returns → *then* `Close()`. Strict ordering, no race. That is exactly the path this branch's graceful Quit buys — so the fix is soundly reasoned, not cargo-culted.

What #1599 left behind is the sibling case: `shutdown(kill=true)` skips the join *entirely*, so no amount of ultraviolet correctness helps. That residual is a very clean upstream change:

```go
if p.cancelReader.Cancel() {
    if !kill { p.waitForReadLoop() }   // tea.go:1251-1254
}
_ = p.cancelReader.Close()
```

`Cancel()` returning true means the read *was* successfully interrupted — the loop is provably waking up right now — and `waitForReadLoop` is already capped at 500ms (`tty.go:97-102`). So the `!kill` guard protects nothing: dropping it costs microseconds in practice and 500ms worst case. The `kill` distinction properly belongs to the renderer stop (skip the final render), not to descriptor teardown. Bubbletea is the right layer, not cancelreader: cancelreader is effectively frozen (v0.2.2 is latest, and `go list -m -versions` confirms no newer release), and ultraviolet already vendors around it. Caching fds at construction in cancelreader would also work but fixes a narrower symptom in a dead repo.

Both deps are at latest (`bubbletea/v2` v2.0.8 is the newest of 12 published v2 versions), so there is no version bump that fixes this today.

**An upstream fix deletes this workaround completely**: the `killCtx` indirection, the watcher goroutine, `loginURLQuitGrace`, the `closeTTY = false` branch, and the `tea.ErrProgramKilled` check all go away, and `readLoginURLActionFromTTY` returns to `tea.WithContext(ctx)` plus a plain `defer tty.Close()`. Given that, the code should carry a pointer to #1599 and the follow-up so the deletion is discoverable — right now nothing in the comments says "this is temporary."

## 4. Durability — where it belongs

There is **no** TUI or Bubble Tea section in `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` today. `tea.`/Bubble Tea appears only twice, both incidental: `CLAUDE.md:744` lists Bubble Tea among terminal-gated paths to inspect for the *agent-safe fallbacks* rule, and the `/dev/tty` mentions at `:321-340` are about `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` detection, not program lifecycle. Neither is the right home.

The right home is a new `#### TUI Programs (Bubble Tea)` subsection under `## Code Patterns`, sitting beside `#### go-git v5 Bugs - Use CLI Instead`. That existing entry is the exact template: a named third-party bug, a "use X instead" prescription, and a forbidigo rule enforcing it. ## Verdict summary

All the machinery this diff adds around `program.Run()` collapses to **two lines**. I verified the collapsed form compiles, vets clean, and passes `TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY*` + `TestWaitForLoginURLResult*` at `-count=800` under `-race` (and the intermediate variant at `-count=1200`), in a throwaway worktree at `9cebf4abb`.

### 1. The watchdog goroutine — `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-fix-login-tty-test-race/cmd/entire/cli/login.go:770-796`

**Summary:** a 21-line channel/select/nested-goroutine assembly that `context.AfterFunc` expresses in two lines.

- **(a) `case <-runDone: return`** — not load-bearing for behaviour. If `ctx` fires after `Run` returned, `program.Quit()` is already a no-op (`Send` selects on `p.ctx.Done()`, and `shutdown` calls `p.cancel()` before `Run` returns), and the *inner* `case <-runDone` already short-circuits. Its only job is avoiding a goroutine parked forever on a `ctx` that never cancels — real (`TestReadLoginURLActionFromTTY_SingleKey…` passes `context.Background()`, and `startActionRead` re-enters this function after every copy), but it is hygiene, not logic. `context.AfterFunc` removes the need entirely: with a `context.Background()` parent, `propagateCancel` sees `done == nil` and registers *nothing* — zero goroutines, versus one per call today.
- **(b) `go program.Quit()`** — necessary *only because the fallback exists*. `Quit` blocks on an unbuffered `p.msgs`, so calling it inline would prevent the same goroutine from reaching `time.After`. Delete the fallback (see #2) and the inner goroutine goes with it. If you keep a deadline, `time.AfterFunc` inverts the nesting instead: arm the timer, then call `Quit` inline.
- **(c) Flattened, equivalent:**

```go
	program := tea.NewProgram(
		loginURLActionModel{},
		tea.WithInput(tty),
		tea.WithOutput(io.Discard),
		tea.WithoutSignalHandler(),
	)

	// Cancellation must reach Bubble Tea as a Quit, never as its context: Run
	// treats a cancelled context as a kill, and shutdown(kill=true) skips
	// waitForReadLoop() before closing its cancelreader — closing tty, and
	// cancelreader's own cancel-signal pipe, under a live reader. A QuitMsg
	// leaves `killed` false, so the read loop is joined before anything closes.
	stopQuit := context.AfterFunc(ctx, program.Quit)
	defer stopQuit()

	finalModel, err := program.Run()
```

Gone: `killCtx`/`kill`, `tea.WithContext`, `runDone`, `close(runDone)`, both selects, both goroutines, `time.After`, and the `loginURLQuitGrace` const. **Measured: 46 lines removed, 9 added.** What it loses: nothing I could find or provoke — see #2.

---

### 2. Is the fallback worth its cost? — `login.go:751-760, 780-792` + const at `login.go:65-69`

**Verdict: remove it.** Not "unobserved, therefore probably fine" — I probed it, and **it does not do the thing it exists to do.**

I built a model that blocks forever inside `Update` (the only way an event loop can refuse a `QuitMsg`), then reproduced the shipped watchdog exactly — `go program.Quit()`, wait, `kill()`:

```
zzz_killctx_probe_test.go:62: kill() did NOT unblock Run on a wedged event loop
```

`kill()` cancels the program context, but `eventLoop` observes that only at its `select`; wedged inside `Update` it never gets back there, so `Run` never returns and `finishActionRead` blocks anyway. The 2s grace buys a 2s delay before the same stranded sign-in. (`program.Kill()` fails identically — probed.)

The structural argument, from upstream source: `Quit` = `select { <-p.ctx.Done(); p.msgs <- msg }`, and `p.msgs` has exactly one receiver (`tea.go:752`). So `Quit` blocks only while `Run` is (i) in setup before `eventLoop`, (ii) inside the loop body, or (iii) between `eventLoop` and `shutdown`'s `p.cancel()`. In (iii) `Quit` unblocks within microseconds and `Run` is already returning. In (i) the loop parks and takes the `QuitMsg`; a setup hang is a syscall (`initTerminal`, `GetSize`) that context cancellation cannot interrupt. In (ii) a body that returns lets `Quit` land unaided; a body that never returns defeats the fallback — verified above. **There is no state in which the fallback converts a hang into a non-hang.**

Worse, its one *reachable* effect is negative: a graceful shutdown that is slow but finite (>2s) gets converted into a killed `Run` — precisely the `shutdown(kill=true)` path this fix exists to stop taking, plus a leaked fd.

Removing it deletes: `killCtx`/`kill`/`defer kill()`, `tea.WithContext`, the nested select, `time.After`, the `loginURLQuitGrace` const and its 4-line comment, and the inner goroutine. `closeTTY` and the `errors.Is` check **stay** (see #3) — so that cost was never really the fallback's.

Also worth stating in the PR: the fallback is untestable as written. Nothing in the package can reach it, because the model is hard-wired inside the function with no seam. 20 lines of insurance with zero coverage and a probe showing it doesn't fire usefully is the case for deletion, not for a test.

**Summary:** keep the bool; it is the clearest form. The alternative (`errors.Is` inside the deferred close, over a function-scope `runErr`) is the same two-site shape with a wider variable and buries the intent in the cause. `closeTTY := true` / `closeTTY = false` is the standard Go rollback-flag idiom.

A tty read failure (pty master revoked, SIGHUP) therefore lands here with the read loop unjoined, exactly as the branch assumes. Keep it, drop the false "only reachable" claim (see #7).

Maintenance cost that does drop out: with #1 applied, declaration and assignment move from 67 lines apart to ~35.

Cheaper too — `AfterFunc` registers nothing when the parent can't be cancelled, where my watchdog spawned a goroutine per call, and this function is re-entered after every copy action.

## Also fixed

`closeTTY` **stays**, but my comment was wrong twice: `Run` wraps *any* event-loop error as `ErrProgramKilled`, and `readLoop` feeds input-stream failures into `p.errs`, so a revoked pty or SIGHUP lands there with the read loop unjoined. Load-bearing, unrelated to the fallback.

Comment triplication collapsed to single homes; dropped "no care on this side avoids it", which sat beside the code that does avoid it; test assertion switched to `Stat` + `os.ErrClosed`, matching the sibling test 130 lines up.

## Three follow-ups I did not fold in

- `review/tui_sink.go` calls `Kill()` at three sites, taking the same kill path. `os.Stdin` means the fd half can't bite, but the upstream cancel-pipe race applies to any `*os.File` input — and its tests use `bytes.NewReader(nil)`, which routes to the no-op fallback reader, so `-race` can never catch it there.
- Nine `tea.NewProgram` sites, five hand-rolled cancellation designs, two worse than the one I fixed. `review` and `login` independently picked the same 2s constant, which is the argument for a shared wrapper plus a `forbidigo` rule.
- Upstream **#1599** (verified: closed 2026-04-13) fixed the sibling half; the pinned ultraviolet does join its inner reader. Dropping bubbletea's `!kill` guard around `waitForReadLoop()` would delete this workaround entirely.

#1981 is still open and still needs a trail approval.

All three PRs are merged and the stale comments are gone from main. Here's what's actually left.

## The reporter still can't get the fix

No tag contains it. Latest nightly is `v0.10.1-nightly.202608180612` (06:19 today); #1981 merged at 08:21. Latest stable is still v0.10.0.

```
$ git tag --contains 976fd4261
(nothing)
```

So Ravikanth is still on `entire login --device` until the next nightly picks it up. He's been waiting since Aug 13 — worth telling him it's landed and which build to grab.

## The question underneath his bug is still unanswered

`CanPromptInteractively()` probes `/dev/tty`, which on Windows resolves to `C:\dev\tty`. That's why his machine got the browser flow and your colleague's clean VM got the device flow. Nobody ran the one command that settles it:

```powershell
Test-Path C:\dev\tty
```

This matters because it decides whether the Windows fix helps most Windows users or only ones with a stray `C:\dev`. And it gates 61 call sites — every wizard, picker, and confirm on Windows is currently on or off by accident.

## Flake status: clean, but not yet proof

Every main run since #2009 landed is green (8/8, one in progress). Honest caveat: the flake was roughly 1-in-tens, so nine runs is consistent with fixed rather than evidence of it. The structural argument is the stronger one — nothing closes a descriptor under a live reader any more.

## Engineering follow-ups, none started

All flagged in #2011's body so they're discoverable:

1. **`review/tui_sink.go`** still calls `Kill()` at `:193`, `:310`, `:316` — same `shutdown(kill=true)` path. `os.Stdin` means the fd half can't bite, but the upstream cancel-pipe race applies to any `*os.File` input, and its tests pass `bytes.NewReader(nil)` so `-race` can never catch it there.
2. **A `uiform.RunProgram(ctx, model, opts...)` wrapper + a `forbidigo` rule on `tea.WithContext`** — nine `tea.NewProgram` sites, five hand-rolled cancellation designs, two worse than the one I fixed. This is the change that makes the hazard unreachable rather than fixed-once.
3. **CLAUDE.md has no TUI section** — this invariant lives only in one function's comment.
4. **Upstream bubbletea**: dropping the `!kill` guard around `waitForReadLoop()` deletes the workaround entirely. `Cancel()` returning true already means the loop is waking, and the join is capped at 500ms.

If you only do one, I'd do #2 — it's the one that stops a future TUI author reproducing this by reaching for the obvious API. But the reporter message costs nothing and unblocks a real person today.
